timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Stewie, I keep hearing about binary. It's just 1s and 0s right? How hard can it be?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Peter, binary is the language of computers. Everything you do on your phone, every photo, every message - it's all just 1s and 0s at the lowest level.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Wait, so my selfies are just a bunch of numbers?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. Each pixel in a photo is represented by binary values for red, green, and blue. A single 4K image contains billions of bits.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Here's where it gets interesting for security. Binary is where vulnerabilities like buffer overflows happen. When data overflows its allocated memory, it can overwrite adjacent binary data.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: It is. And that's exactly how attackers gain remote code execution. They carefully craft binary payloads that overwrite return addresses on the stack.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Understanding hexadecimal helps too - it's just a compact way to represent binary. Instead of writing 10101011, you write AB.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Is this something I need for a cybersecurity job?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Absolutely. A common interview question is: explain how data is represented in binary and why this matters for security. Knowing binary is fundamental to reverse engineering, exploit development, and forensics.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Key takeaway: binary is the foundation of all digital data. Every cybersecurity concept builds on understanding how data is represented at this level.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Okay, I'll never look at a JPEG the same way again.
